chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazal, from Ali ibn Uqba, from Bureyd ibn Muawiya, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'A man bequeathed to me (to be an executor), so I asked that he should associate with me a near relative of his. So he did it, and he, the one who bequeathed to me, mentioned that for him with the one who is an associate with regards to the bequest, are one hundred and fifty Dirhams as security, a bowl of silver. So when the man died, the executor said that he has a claim against him (the deceased) a certain measurements of wheat.'
He (peace be upon him) said: 'If he establishes the evidence, otherwise there is nothing for him.'
I said to him, 'Is it permissible for him that he takes anything from what is in his hands?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not permissible for him.'

I said, 'What is your view, if that man is inimical towards him, so he takes his wealth, and he is able to take from his wealth what he takes, that would be for him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'This (situation) is not similar to this.'
ai.seo_question: Can an executor deduct their own debt from a security deposit held for the deceased without evidence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principle of 'holding in trust' (istid'af) versus 'right of retention' (haqq al-qabd), establishing that an executor cannot unilaterally convert a security deposit into payment for an unproven debt. The Imam distinguishes this legal retention from forcible seizure by an enemy, emphasizing that while force bypasses procedural proof, contractual or fiduciary retention requires valid evidence to justify appropriating the asset.
